problemStatement: Pulsars — rotating, magnetized neutron stars that emit beamed electromagnetic radiation — are among the most extreme objects in the universe, yet the detailed physical pathways by which they form remain incompletely understood. The central question is: through which astrophysical channels are pulsars born, and what physical parameters (progenitor mass, explosion mechanism, binary interaction, magnetic field amplification) determine whether the resulting neutron star is observed as a normal radio pulsar, a millisecond pulsar, a magnetar, or a member of a double neutron star binary? Answering this question requires integrating stellar evolution, core-collapse supernova physics, binary population synthesis, and magnetohydrodynamics into a unified framework that can be tested against the growing multi-messenger pulsar census.
technicalDetails: Pulsar formation is understood to proceed through at least four distinct channels: (1) the canonical iron core-collapse of massive stars (M ≳ 8–10 M☉), in which the proto-neutron star is born with natal spin periods of ~10–100 ms, surface magnetic fields of ~10^12 G, and kick velocities of ~100–1000 km/s imparted by asymmetric neutrino emission and/or hydrodynamic instabilities (Janka 2004; Janka, Kifonidis & Rampp 2001; Cerdá-Durán & Elias-Rosa 2018); (2) electron-capture supernovae in super-AGB stars (M ~ 8–10 M☉), which produce neutron stars with characteristically low kicks and may explain the existence of wide binary pulsars (Stevenson et al. 2022); (3) accretion-induced collapse (AIC) of white dwarfs exceeding the Chandrasekhar mass, producing slowly rotating, weakly magnetized neutron stars that may later be recycled (Zhu, Lu & Wang 2015); and (4) the recycling channel, in which an old neutron star in a low-mass X-ray binary accretes matter and angular momentum from a companion star, spinning up to millisecond periods — this requires a minimum accretion rate above ~10^{-3} of the Eddington limit (Pan, Zhang & Wang 2013). For the most strongly magnetized pulsars (magnetars, B ~ 10^14–10^15 G), additional formation channels have been proposed: convective dynamos in rapidly rotating proto-neutron stars (Raynaud et al. 2020), binary tidal spin-up, common-envelope evolution, and stellar mergers (Hu & Zhang 2025). The relative contributions of these channels remain observationally unconstrained. Rate-comparison arguments (Portegies Zwart & van den Heuvel 1999) show that the bulk of single radio pulsars must come from core-collapse supernovae of single massive stars, but the fractions contributed by ECSNe, AIC, and binary channels are still debated. Double neutron star systems — in which both components are pulsars — require two consecutive supernova explosions in a massive binary (Fröhlich, Regály & Vinkó 2023), adding further complexity to the formation picture.

datasets.source: Published pulsar catalogs (ATNF Pulsar Catalogue), supernova remnant surveys, gravitational-wave transient catalogs (LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA O1–O4), and Gaia astrometric data for pulsar proper motions and distances.
datasets.target: Constrained formation channel fractions for four pulsar sub-populations: (i) normal isolated radio pulsars from iron core-collapse SNe, (ii) pulsars from electron-capture SNe, (iii) millisecond pulsars from the recycling channel, and (iv) magnetars from dynamo and binary merger channels.

paperTitle: Unified Formation Channels of Pulsars: From Core Collapse to Recycling — A Multi-Messenger Population Synthesis Approach
paperAbstract: We present a comprehensive study of pulsar formation channels by integrating state-of-the-art core-collapse supernova simulations, binary population synthesis, and magnetohydrodynamic dynamo models. Pulsars are born through at least four distinct pathways: canonical iron core-collapse of massive stars, electron-capture supernovae in super-AGB stars, accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs, and the recycling of old neutron stars via binary accretion. Using multi-messenger observational constraints — including the ATNF pulsar catalog, gravitational-wave binary neutron star merger rates, Gaia proper motions, and supernova remnant associations — we construct a unified population synthesis framework that self-consistently predicts the birth properties (mass, spin, magnetic field, kick velocity) of neutron stars across all channels. We find that core-collapse supernovae dominate the formation of normal radio pulsars, while electron-capture supernovae contribute a subdominant but observable population of low-kick wide binary pulsars. Millisecond pulsar formation requires sustained accretion above a critical rate threshold, and magnetar formation can proceed through both isolated convective-dynamo and binary-merger channels. Our model reproduces the observed pulsar period–magnetic field distribution, the Galactic double neutron star merger rate, and the magnetar-to-pulsar ratio, while making testable predictions for next-generation radio surveys and gravitational-wave detectors.
methods: We employ a three-component methodology: (1) Single-star core-collapse supernova modeling using 3D neutrino-radiation-hydrodynamic simulations (following Janka et al. 2001, Cerdá-Durán & Elias-Rosa 2018) to map progenitor mass ranges to neutron star birth properties (mass, spin period, magnetic field, kick velocity); (2) Binary population synthesis using the COSMIC and MOBSE frameworks (following Portegies Zwart & van den Heuvel 1999, Fröhlich et al. 2023, Stevenson et al. 2022, Zhu et al. 2015) to model the evolution of massive binaries through common-envelope phases, stable mass transfer, and supernova explosions, producing double neutron star systems and predicting the recycled millisecond pulsar population; (3) 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations of proto-neutron star convective dynamos (following Raynaud et al. 2020, Hu & Zhang 2025) to determine the conditions under which magnetar-strength fields (B ≳ 10^14 G) can be generated. These components are combined into a unified Monte Carlo population synthesis code that generates synthetic pulsar populations for each formation channel. The synthetic populations are compared against the ATNF Pulsar Catalogue (period, period derivative, characteristic age, dispersion measure), Gaia DR4 proper motions, LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA binary neutron star merger rate measurements, and supernova remnant–pulsar associations.

baselines: Standard single-channel core-collapse supernova population synthesis (canonical kick distribution, no electron-capture or AIC channels)
Binary population synthesis with only the isolated core-collapse channel for neutron star formation (no recycling)
Magnetar formation via convective dynamo only (no binary merger channel)
Empirical pulsar birth property distributions from the ATNF catalog without physical modeling
metrics: Reproduction of the observed pulsar period–period derivative (P–Ṗ) diagram (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test on log P and log Ṗ distributions)
Galactic double neutron star merger rate (predicted vs. LIGO/Virgo measured 210 Myr⁻¹)
Fraction of high-velocity pulsars (v > 500 km/s) matching Gaia proper motion data
Magnetar-to-normal pulsar ratio in the Galactic disk
Binary pulsar orbital period and eccentricity distributions
Electron-capture supernova contribution to the pulsar population (constrained by wide binary pulsar statistics)
experiments.design: We run the unified population synthesis model with each formation channel toggled on/off in a factorial design: (A) iron core-collapse only, (B) + electron-capture SNe, (C) + AIC, (D) + recycling channel, (E) + magnetar dynamo, (F) full model with all channels. For each configuration we generate 10^6 synthetic pulsars and compare against observational metrics. We perform Bayesian parameter estimation on the channel fractions and birth-property distributions using nested sampling. Falsification criteria: (i) if the full model fails to reproduce the observed P–Ṗ diagram within 2σ, at least one channel assumption is incorrect; (ii) if removing the electron-capture channel does not significantly degrade the fit to wide binary pulsar statistics, ECSNe are not a major formation channel; (iii) if the dynamo model cannot produce sufficient magnetars without fine-tuning initial spin periods below 3 ms, the pure dynamo hypothesis for magnetar formation would be falsified, requiring merger channels to dominate.

results: We expect to find that: (1) canonical iron core-collapse supernovae account for ~70–80% of all Galactic pulsars, producing neutron stars with birth spin periods of 10–100 ms, magnetic fields of 10^11–10^13 G, and a Maxwellian kick velocity distribution with σ ~ 265 km/s; (2) electron-capture supernovae contribute ~5–10% of pulsars, predominantly in wide binaries with low space velocities (< 100 km/s), consistent with the observed population of wide binary pulsars; (3) the recycling channel produces the entire millisecond pulsar population (~15% of all detected pulsars), with a minimum accretion rate threshold that naturally explains the observed gap in the spin-period distribution between normal and millisecond pulsars; (4) magnetars represent ~5–10% of neutron star births, with the convective dynamo channel dominating for isolated magnetars and binary merger channels contributing in old stellar populations; (5) the combined model reproduces the Galactic double neutron star merger rate within the LIGO/Virgo 90% confidence interval. If the electron-capture channel is subdominant (< 2%), this would falsify the super-AGB progenitor hypothesis for wide binary pulsars. If the dynamo model requires initial proto-neutron star spin periods shorter than observationally plausible (< 1 ms), the pure dynamo hypothesis for magnetar formation would be falsified, requiring merger channels to dominate.

references.title: Neutron Star Formation and Birth Properties
references.relevance: Comprehensive theoretical review of neutron star formation covering progenitors, natal masses, spins, magnetic fields, and space velocities — the foundational reference for pulsar birth properties.

references.title: Supernova Explosions and Neutron Star Formation
references.relevance: Reviews the neutrino-driven mechanism for core-collapse supernovae and the formation of neutron stars, providing the physical basis for the primary pulsar formation channel.

references.title: The origin of single radio pulsars
references.relevance: Uses rate-comparison arguments to constrain the progenitor channels of radio pulsars, showing that core-collapse supernovae of single massive stars dominate.

references.title: Magnetar formation through a convective dynamo in protoneutron stars
references.relevance: First 3D simulations demonstrating that convective dynamos in proto-neutron stars can generate magnetar-strength dipolar fields, providing a concrete formation mechanism for the most magnetized pulsars.

references.title: Minimum Accretion Rate for Millisecond Pulsar Formation in Binary System
references.relevance: Identifies the critical accretion rate threshold for recycling neutron stars into millisecond pulsars, a key physical constraint for the MSP formation channel.

references.title: Formation Channels of Magnetars
references.relevance: Systematic review of all magnetar formation channels (isolated core collapse, binary interactions, mergers), highlighting the diversity of pulsar formation pathways.

references.title: Neutron stars formation and Core Collapse Supernovae
references.relevance: Reviews modern observational and theoretical advances in understanding the connection between core-collapse supernovae and neutron star formation.

references.title: Double neutron star formation via consecutive type II supernova explosions
references.relevance: Models the formation of double neutron star systems through two consecutive core-collapse events, a channel that produces binary pulsar systems.

references.title: Wide binary pulsars from electron-capture supernovae
references.relevance: Demonstrates that electron-capture supernovae produce neutron stars with low natal kicks, explaining the observed population of wide binary pulsars as a distinct formation channel.

references.title: Population Synthesis of Millisecond X-ray Pulsars
references.relevance: Population synthesis showing that both core-collapse and accretion-induced collapse channels can produce the observed millisecond X-ray pulsar population, linking formation channels to observables.
